subject: biology

moments.title: Van Leeuwenhoek sees his own dental plaque
moments.body:
Van Leeuwenhoek, the Delft draper and microscopy hobbyist, looks at scrapings of his own teeth under his single-lens microscopes. He sees swarming 'animalcules'. He writes to the Royal Society describing the diverse bacteria of human dental plaque — the first observation of human microbiota.

He also notes that vinegar kills many of them on contact.
moments.takeaway: Three centuries ago, microbes in the human body were observed. Their significance took most of that time to be appreciated.

moments.title: Escherich isolates E. coli
moments.body:
Theodor Escherich isolates and characterises the bacterium that comes to bear his name (Escherichia coli) from infant stool. It becomes the most-studied bacterium in biology — model organism for genetics, biochemistry, and microbiology.

E. coli is one of trillions of bacterial cells in the human gut. The full diversity of the gut microbiome takes another century to begin mapping.
moments.takeaway: Specific human gut bacteria can be cultured and studied. Most can't be — they need their natural community.

moments.title: Gnotobiotic mice
moments.who: Phil Trexler and colleagues, Lobund Institute (Notre Dame)
moments.body:
Researchers raise mice in completely sterile conditions ('germ-free' or gnotobiotic). They show that without bacteria, mice have abnormal immune systems, altered gut development, behavioural changes, and resistance to certain diseases.

Gnotobiotic models become essential tools for understanding the role of microbiota in health.
moments.takeaway: Microbes are not optional inhabitants — they shape the host's biology fundamentally.

moments.title: Human Microbiome Project
moments.body:
The Human Microbiome Project sequences bacteria from healthy volunteers at multiple body sites using 16S ribosomal RNA gene amplification and metagenomics. It reveals enormous diversity: ~10,000+ species in the gut alone, with substantial inter-individual variation.

The European MetaHIT project runs in parallel. Together they establish baselines for healthy human microbiomes and frame disease-associated alterations ('dysbiosis').
moments.takeaway: Human microbiomes are quantitatively defined. Disease patterns can be looked for against a baseline.

moments.title: Faecal microbiota transplant becomes clinical
moments.body:
FMT for recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection is shown effective in randomised trials (van Nood et al., 2013): ~90% cure rate vs ~30% for standard antibiotics. FMT becomes accepted clinical practice for refractory C. difficile.

Trials for other conditions (ulcerative colitis, irritable bowel syndrome, metabolic syndrome, neurodegenerative diseases) are ongoing, with mixed results. The FDA approved two FMT-derived products in 2022-23 (Rebyota, Vowst).
moments.takeaway: Restoring a healthy gut community can cure a stubborn disease. The microbiome is now therapeutic.

now.title: Microbiome today
now.body:
Microbiome research is a major scientific field. We have rich catalogues of gut, skin, oral, vaginal and respiratory microbiomes. Specific bacteria are linked to autoimmune disease, obesity, depression, drug responses.

Industry: probiotic products, personalised microbiome diagnostics, microbe-targeted drugs, faecal transplant capsules.
now.open_questions: Causal effects of microbiome on disease? (Mostly correlations so far.) What are the rules of microbial community assembly? Can we engineer microbiomes for specific outcomes? What's the role of bacteriophages, fungi and protists in the microbiome (mostly understudied)?

reflection: Van Leeuwenhoek saw bacteria in his teeth in 1683. The first hint that they MATTER to human health came centuries later. The full appreciation of the microbiome as a quasi-organ is barely two decades old. How often does science have the evidence but not the framework to recognise importance — and what other 'obvious' things are we still failing to recognise?
